passage:
Age two: at the house of mourning, Jahnavi clung to her mother's leg and watched the weeping adults with wide eyes. Someone whispered, 'Take her out, she shouldn't see this.' Her aunt lifted Jahnavi onto her hip instead and stayed in the room, rocking and humming, saying, 'Everyone is sad. I'm here.' Jahnavi's grip loosened and she rested her head on her aunt's shoulder.

Age sixteen: Kiran's friend Vishal came back to school after his grandfather's funeral. Kiran wanted to help and said, 'At least he lived a long life,' and then, 'It was meant to be.' Vishal's jaw tightened and he looked away. Kiran saw it and felt the words fall flat. Later he said, 'I'm sorry, that wasn't helpful. I'm so sorry about your grandfather. I'm here, whatever you need.' Vishal nodded and sat beside him at lunch.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's aunt do instead of taking her out?
qa.a: She lifted Jahnavi onto her hip and stayed in the room, rocking and humming.

qa.q: How do the two scenes show what helps and what hurts near grief?
qa.a: The aunt lifted Jahnavi onto her hip and stayed in the room, humming, and the child's grip loosened. Kiran's words 'At least he lived a long life' and 'It was meant to be' made Vishal look away until Kiran said he was sorry and that he was there

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he tightened his jaw and looked away?
qa.a: Hurt and sad, since the phrases seemed to make light of his loss.

qa.q: What could Kiran say next time to a grieving friend?
qa.a: Something plain like 'I'm so sorry' and 'I'm here', and then sit quietly beside him.

grounding: A toddler near mourning is comforted by presence at two, and a teenager learns that well-meant phrases can hurt a grieving friend at sixteen.

passage:
Age ten: on Eid morning Rajni carried a covered plate of sheer khurma to the neighbours' flat, careful on the stairs. 'Eid Mubarak, Aunty!' At Diwali the same neighbours came up with a box of sweets, and at Christmas both families ate cake from one plate. Rajni thought the whole building felt like one big house.

Age twenty: Ishita asked her friend if she could come to the Sunday service at the church. On her friend's advice she wore a scarf, took her seat quietly at the back and did not try to join the prayers. Afterwards she asked, 'May I ask what the last part means?' Her friend said, 'Thank you for asking. Not everyone does.'

Age twenty-five: Shreya and her partner, whose faiths differ, sat with two cups of tea and a list: names, which rites, what to tell the children. They did not try to win each point. They agreed to hear both families out and to visit both places of worship together. 'Our parents are worried,' Shreya said. 'Let's be clear early, and kind.'

qa.q: What did Rajni carry to the neighbours on Eid morning?
qa.a: A covered plate of sheer khurma.

qa.q: How does contact across faiths grow from age ten to twenty-five?
qa.a: Rajni carried sheer khurma to the neighbours and later shared sweets and Christmas cake, so the building felt like one big house. Ishita went to a friend's service and only asked questions, and Shreya and her partner made a list and agreed to hear both families out and to be kind

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she said, 'Our parents are worried'?
qa.a: Concerned about the families' reactions, yet wanting to handle it with clarity and kindness.

qa.q: How did Ishita show respect when visiting her friend's church?
qa.a: She asked her friend about etiquette, dressed as advised, sat quietly and asked a question afterwards without trying to join in.

grounding: Interfaith friendship at ten, twenty and twenty-five: sharing festival sweets, respectful curiosity without conversion, and a couple negotiating early.

passage:
Age fifteen: after three videos on electricity, Lokesh told the class, 'The teacher's wrong. Current doesn't get used up.' The teacher smiled. 'Then what does the bulb use?' Lokesh opened his mouth and found he had no answer. His ears went hot.

Age twenty: Urmila learned a project framework in a weekend workshop and felt like an expert. For three weeks she corrected her classmates. Then her team's real project hit a supplier delay, and the framework's neat boxes did not fit. Her confidence dropped, and she felt she knew nothing. She began asking the seniors detailed questions, and her skill began to grow.

Age twenty-five: Uma, a young engineer, solved bugs that stumped others in minutes. 'It's easy, anyone can do it,' she said, and privately wondered whether she belonged. A colleague said, 'It took me two days last week.' Uma blinked. She started noticing the gaps in her own knowledge, stopped brushing off what she did well, and began teaching the fix to others.

qa.q: What question did the teacher ask Lokesh about the bulb?
qa.a: 'Then what does the bulb use?'

qa.q: How does confidence relate to real skill at fifteen, twenty and twenty-five?
qa.a: Lokesh felt like an expert after three videos but could not answer a basic question. Urmila felt expert after a workshop until a real project dropped her confidence before her skill grew, and Uma, truly skilled, assumed her fixes were easy and doubted herself.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling as his ears went hot?
qa.a: Embarrassed, as he realised he did not know as much as he had claimed.

qa.q: What could Urmila do during the dip in confidence?
qa.a: Keep asking the seniors detailed questions and treat the dip as a normal sign that she is learning.

grounding: Overconfidence after a few videos at fifteen, the dip after early expertise at twenty, and a skilled engineer underrating herself at twenty-five.

passage:
Age nine: Indu got four out of ten in the spelling test and threw her paper down. 'The teacher is mean. I got low marks because they don't like me.' She had not opened her spelling notebook all week. Her mother asked, 'Which words did you get wrong?' Indu shrugged.

Age fifteen: when his parents argued in the kitchen, Hrithik lay in bed and told himself it was his fault: if his marks were better, if he had not asked for a new phone. That night he apologised to his mother for a quarrel she had with his father. His mother hugged him. 'This one isn't yours to fix.'

Age twenty-five: Chinmay lost a third job in two years. 'The boss hated me, the market is bad, and it's just my luck,' he told his roommate. His roommate asked, 'Is there anything you would do differently?' Chinmay's answer was quick. 'No.' A week later, alone with the latest rejection email, he wrote a list of what he did control: his CV, his skills, the calls he could make.

qa.q: How many marks did Indu get in the spelling test?
qa.a: Four out of ten.

qa.q: How do the beliefs about control differ across nine, fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: Indu blamed the teacher and never linked her marks with her unopened notebook. Hrithik blamed himself for his parents' argument, and Chinmay blamed the boss, the market and luck, so each view was lopsided in a different way.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he lay in bed during his parents' argument?
qa.a: Guilty and responsible for something that was not his to fix.

qa.q: What could Chinmay ask himself next time a job ends?
qa.a: What his own share was and what he can change, as his list of things he controls began to show.

grounding: Locus of control at nine, fifteen and twenty-five: blaming the teacher, blaming oneself for family conflict, and blaming others for repeated setbacks.

passage:
Age nine: Leela listened to the tired teacher's flat voice through the last period and thought, this teacher is bored with us. Then the teacher stayed after class to help Leela with a sum and said, in the same flat voice, 'You are getting there.' Leela realised the voice was simply how the teacher sounded when tired.

Age fifteen: Aadhya spoke so softly in class that people leaned in. The teacher wrote 'low confidence' in her report. Her cousin said, 'At home you're loud!' Aadhya told a friend that speaking up in a big room made her chest tight. When she was allowed to answer in a small group first, her voice grew.

Age twenty-five: Gautam worked in a mixed team with colleagues from three countries. He found one group's loud lunchtime talk friendly, while another colleague read it as anger. A softly spoken colleague seemed shy to him until she said, 'Where I grew up, soft is respectful.' Gautam stopped judging character by volume and started asking.

qa.q: What did the teacher write in Aadhya's report?
qa.a: 'Low confidence'.

qa.q: How do the three scenes show that voice cues should not be read alone?
qa.a: Leela's teacher's flat voice came from tiredness, not lack of care. Aadhya's soft voice came from a tight chest in a big room, not low confidence, and at Gautam's work loud or soft talk meant friendliness, anger or respect depending on the person's background.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling in the big room?
qa.a: Anxious and self-conscious, with a tight chest.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Aadhya speak up?
qa.a: Offer a small group or quieter setting before the whole class, with encouragement instead of criticism.

grounding: Flat, quiet and loud voices at nine, fifteen and twenty-five that do not reliably show boredom, low confidence, anger or shyness.

passage:
At sixteen, Tanvir's friend Kunal stormed up to him at the school gate. 'You told everyone my results!' Tanvir felt the urge to explain that it was not him. He bit it back. 'Go on, I'm listening.' Kunal shouted for a full minute about the whole class laughing, and Tanvir nodded. 'I can see you're really upset.' Kunal's shoulders dropped. 'Yeah.' After a moment he said, 'It just felt so unfair.' Then Tanvir said, 'It wasn't me, but I get why you thought so. Let's find out who did.'

At twenty-five, Tanvir, now a customer support lead, took a call from an angry client, Sarika. 'This is the third time I've been sent the wrong part!' Tanvir kept his voice low and slow. 'You're right to be frustrated. Three wrong parts is not acceptable. What would help most right now?' Sarika paused. 'A replacement by Friday and one person I can call.' Tanvir wrote it down, repeated it back and promised the call. Sarika's voice was quiet when they ended.

qa.q: What did Kunal accuse Tanvir of?
qa.a: Telling everyone about his results.

qa.q: What do Tanvir's two conversations share?
qa.a: In both he let the angry person be heard first, named the upset, and only then moved to solving it: with Kunal, finding out who told, and with Sarika, asking what would help most. The heat dropped because they felt heard.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when his shoulders dropped?
qa.a: Relief at being heard, though he was still hurt about the class laughing.

qa.q: Why was it useful for Tanvir to repeat Sarika's request back?
qa.a: It showed he had heard the client and made sure the promise matched what was asked for.

grounding: Listening first to an angry friend at sixteen and de-escalating an angry client at twenty-five, where feeling heard comes before problem-solving.
